title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 854–856 (Night 194, continuing nights-193), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 194 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The Lady Budūr tells her foster brother Marzawān her story: she woke in the last third of a night to find beside her a youth of indescribable beauty, took him for a test set by her father, who had pressed her to marry, and so neither woke him nor touched him; in the morning she found his ring on her hand in place of her own. Since then she has neither slept nor done anything but weep and recite verses, and she recites seven lines on the absent beloved. Marzawān, at a loss, promises to travel through every land in search of a cure; she sees him off with three more lines. He journeys a month from city to city and island to island, hearing everywhere of Budūr’s madness, until in the city of al-Ṭayrab he hears that Qamar al-Zamān, son of King Shahramān, lies sick with melancholy and madness in the Islands of Khālidān, a month away by sea. He takes ship; after a month of fair wind, with the islands in sight and only the landing left, a storm strikes, brings down the masts, tears the sails and overturns the ship with all aboard, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالتِّسْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu wa-al-tisʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth and the ninety after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and ninety-fourth night,
sentences.n: al-rābiʿa, “the fourth”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-tisʿūna, “and the ninety”, and baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”, as in the nights before. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ مَرْزَوَانَ قَالَ لِلسَّيِّدَةِ بُدُورَ أَخْبِرِينِي بِقِصَّتِكِ وَمَا اتَّفَقَ لَكِ لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ أَنْ يُطْلِعَنِي عَلَى مَا فِيهِ خَلَاصُكِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Marzawāna qāla li-al-sayyidati Budūra akhbirīnī bi-qiṣṣatiki wa-mā ittafaqa laki laʿalla Allāha an yuṭliʿanī ʿalā mā fīhi khalāṣuki
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Marzawān said to-the-lady Budūr: Inform-me of-your-story and-what befell to-you; perhaps God that He-let-me-see onto what in-it (is) your-deliverance.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Marzawān said to the Lady Budūr, “Tell me your story and all that has happened to you; it may be that God will show me the way to set you free.”
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the night with Marzawān’s request, which closed the last one, in slightly different words. The print sets السعيدان solid, al-saʿīdu and anna run together as one word; the spacing is kept. akhbara bi-, Form IV, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news, here “your story”. ittafaqa li-, Form VIII, “to happen to”: li- marks the one it happens to. laʿalla Allāha an yuṭliʿanī: once more an after laʿalla, a Middle Arabic habit met in the last night. aṭlaʿa ʿalā, Form IV, “to let (someone) see, acquaint (someone) with”. mā fīhi khalāṣuki, “that in which is your deliverance”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ يَا أَخِي اسْمَعْ قِصَّتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-sittu Budūru yā akhī ismaʿ qiṣṣatī
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-Lady Budūr: O my-brother, hear my-story.
sentences.i: The Lady Budūr said to him, “Brother, hear my story.
sentences.n: Marzawān is her foster brother, nursed at the same breast, so akhī, “my brother”, is meant in earnest. ismaʿ, imperative of samiʿa, “to hear”. The shadda of قصّتي is printed.

sentences.t: وَذٰلِكَ أَنِّي اسْتَيْقَظْتُ مِنْ مَنَامِي لَيْلَةً فِى الثُّلُثِ الْأَخِيرِ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ وَجَلَسْتُ عَلَى حَيْلِي
sentences.tr: wa-dhālika annī istayqaẓtu min manāmī laylatan fī al-thuluthi al-akhīri mina al-layli wa-jalastu ʿalā ḥaylī
sentences.l: And-that (is) that-I awoke from my-sleep one-night in the-third the-last of the-night, and-I-sat on my-strength,
sentences.i: It was like this: one night, in the last third of the night, I woke from my sleep and sat up,
sentences.n: wa-dhālika annī …, “and that is (that) I …”, the teller’s way into an account. laylatan, “one night”, accusative of time. jalasa ʿalā ḥaylihi, “to sit on one’s strength”, a colloquial phrase: to sit up. The print writes fī with ى, فى; it is kept.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرْتُ إِلَى جَانِبِي شَابًّا أَحْسَنَ مَايَكُونُ مِنَ الشَّبَابِ يَكِلُّ عَنْ وَصْفِهِ اللِّسَانُ كَأَنَّهُ غُصْنُ بَانٍ أَوْ قَضِيبُ خَيْزُرَانٍ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓartu ilā jānibī shābban aḥsana mā yakūnu mina al-shabābi yakillu ʿan waṣfihi al-lisānu ka-annahu ghuṣnu bānin aw qaḍību khayzurānin
sentences.l: and-I-looked to my-side: a-youth, (the) fairest (of) what may-be of the-youths, falls-short from describing-him the-tongue, as-if-he (were) a-bough (of) ban or a-rod (of) cane.
sentences.i: and looking to my side I saw a youth, the handsomest that ever was, beyond the power of any tongue to describe, as slender as a branch of the ban tree or a rod of cane.
sentences.n: naẓara ilā takes its object with ilā, so the accusative shābban, “a youth”, hangs on an “I saw” that is left unsaid; a loose but common turn. aḥsana mā yakūnu, “the fairest of what may be”, a superlative with mā; the print runs mā into its verb, مايكون. kalla ʿan, “to grow weary of, fall short of”: the tongue gives up on describing him. The ban (moringa) branch and the cane are stock images of a slender, supple figure. The shaddas of شابّا and يكلّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَظَنَنْتُ أَنَّ أَبِي هُوَ الَّذِي أَمَرَةُ بِهٰذَا الْأَمْرِ لِيَمْتَحِنَنِي بِهِ لِأَنَّهُ رَاوَدَنِي عَنِ الزَّوَاجِ لَمَّا خَطَبَنِى مِنْهُ الْمُلُوكُ فَأَبَيْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-ẓanantu anna abī huwa alladhī amarahu bi-hādhā al-amri li-yamtaḥinanī bihi li-annahu rāwadanī ʿani al-zawāji lammā khaṭabanī minhu al-mulūku fa-abaytu
sentences.l: And-I-thought that my-father, he (was) the-one-who ordered-him with-this the-matter, to-test-me with-it, because-he had-pressed-me about the-marriage when sought-me-in-marriage from-him the-kings, and-I-refused.
sentences.i: I thought it was my father who had put him up to this, to test me, because he had pressed me to marry when the kings sought my hand from him, and I refused.
sentences.n: The print has فطننت, a misprint for فظننت, “and I thought”, corrected here. amara bi-, “to order (someone) to do”: the verb takes the thing ordered with bi-. The print writes the pronoun of amarahu, “ordered him”, with ة, امرة, as it does now and then. imtaḥana bi-, Form VIII, “to test (someone) by”: bi- marks the means. rāwada ʿan, Form III, “to try to talk (someone) into”, a verb more often used of seduction. khaṭaba … min, “to ask for (a woman) in marriage from (her father)”; the print writes the -nī of خطبنى with ى. Budūr had refused the kings who asked for her, as the jinn told it some nights back.

sentences.t: فَهٰذَا الظَّنُّ هُوَ الَّذِي مَنَعَنِي مِنْ أَنْ أُنَبِّهَهُ وَخَشِيتُ أَنِّي إِذَا عَمِلْتُ شَيْأً أَوْ إِعَانَتَةُ رُبَّمَا يُخْبِرُ لِأَبِي بِذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-hādhā al-ẓannu huwa alladhī manaʿanī min an unabbihahu wa-khashītu annī idhā ʿamiltu shayʾan aw iʿānatahu rubbamā yukhbiru li-abī bi-dhālika
sentences.l: So-this the-suspicion, it (is) what kept-me from that I-wake-him; and-I-feared that-I, if I-did something or his-helping, perhaps he-would-tell to-my-father of-that.
sentences.i: It was this suspicion that kept me from waking him; and I was afraid that if I did anything, or gave him any help, he might tell my father of it.
sentences.n: nabbaha, Form II, “to wake, rouse”. annī idhā …, “that I, if …”: the clause begun with “I” is never finished, and a new subject takes over, “perhaps he would tell”; loose, as speech is. اعانتة is doubtful. Read as printed it is iʿānatahu, “helping him”, a verbal noun with the pronoun spelled ة, standing loosely as a second object of ʿamiltu; but the sense seems to want something warmer, and the likeliest candidate is اعانقه, uʿāniquhu, “I embrace him”, with ت set for ق. The print’s letters are kept and read as iʿānatahu. akhbara takes the person told as its direct object in Classical Arabic; here li-, “to”, marks him, yukhbiru li-abī, as in the spoken language, and bi- marks the news. The hamza of شيأ is printed, on the alif of the accusative.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحْتُ رَأَيْتُ بِيَدِي خَاتَمَهُ عِوَضًا عَنْ خَاتَمِي الَّذِي أَخَذَةُ مِنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥtu raʾaytu bi-yadī khātamahu ʿiwaḍan ʿan khātamī alladhī akhadhahu minnī
sentences.l: And-when I-reached-morning, I-saw on-my-hand his-ring in-exchange for my-ring which he-took-it from-me.
sentences.i: When morning came, I saw his ring on my hand in place of my own, which he had taken from me.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa, Form IV, “to reach the morning”. bi-yadī, “on my hand”: bi- of place. ʿiwaḍan ʿan, “in exchange for, in place of”. akhadhahu, “he took it”: the print writes the pronoun with ة again, اخذة. The hamza of رأيت is printed.

sentences.t: فَهٰذِةِ حِكَايَتِي وَسَبَبُ جُنُونِي
sentences.tr: fa-hādhihi ḥikāyatī wa-sababu junūnī
sentences.l: So-this (is) my-story and-(the) cause (of) my-madness.
sentences.i: That is my story, and the cause of my madness.
sentences.n: The print spells hādhihi with ة, هذة, as it does throughout this night.

sentences.t: وَأَنَايَا أَخِي قَدْ تَعَلَّقَ قَلْبِي بِهِ مِنْ حِينِ رُؤْيَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-anā yā akhī qad taʿallaqa qalbī bihi min ḥīni ruʾyatihi
sentences.l: And-I, O my-brother, has clung my-heart to-him from (the) time (of) seeing-him,
sentences.i: And I, brother, have had my heart bound to him from the moment I saw him,
sentences.n: The print runs anā and yā together, وانايا; the spacing is kept. anā stands first as a topic, and the sentence goes on with “my heart”. taʿallaqa bi-, Form V, “to cling to, become attached to”: bi- marks what is clung to. ruʾyatihi, “the seeing of him”, the verbal noun with its object as a suffix. The ؤ of رؤيته is printed.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ كَثْرَةِ عِشْقِي وَالْغَرَامِ لَمْ أَذُقْ طَعْمَ الْمَنَامِ وَمَالِي شُغْلٌ غَيْرُ الدُّمُوعِ وَالْبُكَاءِ وَإِنْشَادِ الْأَشْعَارِ بِاللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-min kathrati ʿishqī wa-al-gharāmi lam adhuq ṭaʿma al-manāmi wa-mā lī shughlun ghayru al-dumūʿi wa-al-bukāʾi wa-inshādi al-ashʿāri bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri
sentences.l: and-from (the) muchness (of) my-love and-the-passion not I-tasted (the) taste (of) the-sleep, and-not for-me (is) occupation other-than the-tears and-the-weeping and-reciting the-poems by-the-night and-the-day.
sentences.i: and for the greatness of my love and longing I have not tasted the taste of sleep, and I have nothing to do but shed tears and weep and recite poems by night and by day.”
sentences.n: She falls into rhyme: gharām, manām; then nahār. min, “from”, gives the cause. lam adhuq, jussive of dhāqa, “to taste”. mā lī, “I have not”, literally “not for me”, run together in the print as ومالي. ghayru, “other than”, agrees with shughlun, “occupation”, and the things excepted follow in the genitive. bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri, “by night and by day”: bi- of time.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَفَاضَتِ الْعَبَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ هٰذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma afāḍati al-ʿabarāti wa-anshadat hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then she-poured-forth the-tears and-recited these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then she let her tears flow, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: afāḍa, Form IV, “to make overflow, pour out”, takes the tears as its object; ʿabarāt is a feminine plural, so its accusative ends in -i. hādhihi is spelled with ة again, هذة.

sentences.t:
اَبَعْدَ الْحِبِّ لَذَّاتِي تَطِيبُ * وَذَاكَ الظَّبْيُ مَرْتَعُهُ الْقُلُوبُ
دَمُ الْعُشَّاقِ اَهْوَنُ مَا عَلَيْه * وَفِيهِ مُهْجَةُ الْمُضْنَى تَذُوبُ
اَغَارُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ نَظَرِي وَفِكْرِي * فَمِنْ بَعْضِي عَلَى بَعْضِي رَقِيبُ
وَاَجْفَانٍ لَهُ تَرْمِي سِهَامًا * فَوَاتِكَ فِي الْقُلُوبِ لَنَا تُصِيبُ
فَهَلْ لِي اَنْ اَرَاةُ قُبَيْلَ مَوْتِي * اِذَا مَا كَانَ فِي الدُّنْيَا نَصِيبُ
وَاَكْتُمُ سِرَّهُ فَيَنِمُّ دَمْعِي * بِمَا عِنْدِي وَيَعْلَمُهُ الرَّقِيبُ
قَرِيبٌ وَصْلُهُ مِنِّي بَعِيدٌ * بَعِيدٌ ذِكْرُهُ مِنِّي قَرِيبُ
sentences.tr:
a-baʿda al-ḥibbi ladhdhātī taṭību * wa-dhāka al-ẓabyu martaʿuhu al-qulūbu
damu al-ʿushshāqi ahwanu mā ʿalayh * wa-fīhi muhjatu al-muḍnā tadhūbu
aghāru ʿalayhi min naẓarī wa-fikrī * fa-min baʿḍī ʿalā baʿḍī raqību
wa-ajfānin lahu tarmī sihāman * fawātika fī al-qulūbi lanā tuṣību
fa-hal lī an arāhu qubayla mawtī * idhā mā kāna fī al-dunyā naṣību
wa-aktumu sirrahu fa-yanimmu damʿī * bi-mā ʿindī wa-yaʿlamuhu al-raqību
qarībun waṣluhu minnī baʿīdun * baʿīdun dhikruhu minnī qarību
sentences.l:
(Is it) after the-beloved (that) my-pleasures are-sweet? * And-that the-gazelle, its-pasture (is) the-hearts.
(The) blood (of) the-lovers (is the) lightest (of) what (is) upon-him, * and-in-him (the) heart’s-blood (of) the-wasted-one melts.
I-am-jealous over-him of my-gaze and-my-thought, * so-of part-of-me over part-of-me (is) a-watcher.
And-(many) eyelids of-his shoot arrows, * deadly-ones, in the-hearts for-us they-hit.
So-is-there for-me that I-see-him a-little-before my-death, * if is in the-world a-share?
And-I-hide his-secret, and-tells-tales my-tears * of-what (is) with-me, and-knows-it the-watcher.
Near: his-union from-me (is) far; * far: his-remembrance from-me (is) near.
sentences.i:
With the beloved gone, can my pleasures still be sweet? * That gazelle has hearts for his pasture.
Lovers’ blood is the least of his cares, * and in him the wasted lover’s heart melts away.
I am jealous over him of my own eyes and thoughts, * so that one part of me stands watch over the other.
His eyelids loose their arrows, * deadly ones that strike home in our hearts.
Might I see him, just once before I die, * if any portion is left me in this world?
I hide his secret, but my tears tell * what is in me, and the watcher knows it.
He is near, yet union with him is far from me; * far, yet the thought of him is near.
sentences.n: The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept. As before it writes hamza as a vowel on bare alif (اَبَعْدَ, اَهْوَنُ, اَنْ, اِذَا), and it leaves the end of the first hemistich of the second line, عَلَيْه, without a vowel. a-, the question prefix, is rhetorical: “are my pleasures sweet after the beloved?” ḥibb, “beloved”. The beloved is a gazelle whose pasture, martaʿ, is hearts. ahwanu mā ʿalayhi, “the lightest thing upon him”, what he cares least about. muhja, “heart’s blood, life”; al-muḍnā, “the one wasted (by love)”, passive participle of aḍnā. ghāra ʿalā … min, “to be jealous over (someone) of (someone)”: she grudges him even her own eyes. wa-ajfānin, “and eyelids”, a genitive after wa-, the wāw of rubba, “and many a …”. fawātik, “deadly”, plural of fātik, a diptote in the accusative to agree with sihāman, “arrows”. In اَرَاةُ the print writes the pronoun of arāhu, “I see him”, with ة, as in the prose, and vowels it as the pronoun. qubayla, diminutive of qabla, “a little before”. naṣīb, “a share, a portion”, of life. namma bi-, “to betray, tell tales of”: bi- marks what is betrayed. The last line turns on near and far: he is near, yet union is far; far, yet the thought of him is near.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ قَالَتْ لِمَرْزَوَانَ انْظُرْ يَا أَخِي مَا الَّذِي تَعْمَلُ مَعِي فِي الَّذِي اعْتَرَانِي
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-sitta Budūra qālat li-Marzawāna unẓur yā akhī mā alladhī taʿmalu maʿī fī alladhī iʿtarānī
sentences.l: Then indeed the-Lady Budūr said to-Marzawān: See, O my-brother, what (is) that-which you-will-do with-me in that-which has-come-upon-me.
sentences.i: Then the Lady Budūr said to Marzawān, “Think, brother, what you can do for me in this that has come upon me.”
sentences.n: thumma inna …, “then (it was so that) …”, the narrator’s usual way of turning the story. li-, “to”, marks the one addressed. ʿamila maʿa, “to do with (someone)”, here to do for. iʿtarā, Form VIII, “to come upon, befall”, as in the last night.

sentences.t: فَأَطْرَقَ مَرْزَوَانُ رَأْسَهُ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ سَاعَةً وَهُوَ يَتَعَجَّبُ وَمَا يَدْرِي مَايَفْعَلُ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭraqa Marzawānu raʾsahu ilā al-arḍi sāʿatan wa-huwa yataʿajjabu wa-mā yadrī mā yafʿalu
sentences.l: So-bowed Marzawān his-head to the-ground an-hour, and-he (was) wondering and-not knowing what he-should-do.
sentences.i: Marzawān bowed his head to the ground for a while, full of wonder and not knowing what to do.
sentences.n: aṭraqa, Form IV, “to bow (the head), look down in silence”, the gesture of one thinking. sāʿatan, “an hour”, a while, accusative of time. wa-huwa …, a circumstantial clause, “while he …”. taʿajjaba, Form V, “to wonder”. The print runs mā into its verb, مايفعل; the spacing is kept. The hamza of رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ وَقَالَ لَهَا جَمِيعُ مَاجَرَى لَكِ صَحِيحٌ وَإِنَّ حِكَايَةَ هٰذَا الشَّابِّ أَعْيَتْ فِكْرِي
sentences.tr: thumma rafaʿa raʾsahu wa-qāla lahā jamīʿu mā jarā laki ṣaḥīḥun wa-inna ḥikāyata hādhā al-shābbi aʿyat fikrī
sentences.l: Then he-raised his-head and-said to-her: All (of) what happened to-you (is) true, and-indeed (the) story (of) this the-youth has-exhausted my-thought.
sentences.i: Then he raised his head and said to her, “All that has happened to you is true, and the story of this young man is beyond my understanding.
sentences.n: jarā li-, “to happen to”: li- marks the one it befalls; the print runs mā into the verb, ماجرى. aʿyā, Form IV, “to tire out, baffle”.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ إِنِّي أَدُورُ فِي جَمِيعِ الْبِلَادِ وَأُفَتِّشُ عَلَى دَوَائِكِ لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يَجْعَلُهُ عَلَى يَدِي وَلٰكِنِ اصْبِرِى وَلَاتَجْزَعِى
sentences.tr: wa-lākin innī adūru fī jamīʿi al-bilādi wa-ufattishu ʿalā dawāʾiki laʿalla Allāha yajʿaluhu ʿalā yadī wa-lākini iṣbirī wa-lā tajzaʿī
sentences.l: But I, I-will-go-round in all the-lands and-search for your-remedy; perhaps God makes-it at my-hand. But be-patient and-do-not despair.
sentences.i: But I will go round all the lands and search for a cure for you; it may be that God will bring it about at my hand. Only be patient, and do not despair.”
sentences.n: wa-lākin innī: Classical Arabic would write wa-lākinnī; here the light lākin is followed by a separate innī. dāra fī, “to go round in”. fattasha ʿalā, Form II, “to search for”, a colloquial construction where Classical says fattasha ʿan, or takes a direct object. jaʿalahu ʿalā yadī, “make it (come) at my hand”, through me. The print writes the feminine endings of iṣbirī and tajzaʿī with ى, اصبرى, تجزعى, and runs lā into its verb, ولاتجزعى; all are kept. The ئ of دوائك is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ مَرْزَوَانَ وَدَّعَهَا وَدَعَا لَهَا بِالثَّبَاتِ وَخَرَجَ مِنْ عِنْدِهَا وَهِيَ تُنْشِدُ هٰذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Marzawāna waddaʿahā wa-daʿā lahā bi-al-thabāti wa-kharaja min ʿindihā wa-hiya tunshidu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then indeed Marzawān bade-her-farewell and-prayed for-her for-the-steadfastness, and-went-out from with-her, and-she (was) reciting these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then Marzawān bade her farewell, prayed that she might be kept steadfast, and went out from her, while she recited these verses:
sentences.n: waddaʿa, Form II, “to bid farewell”; then daʿā li- … bi-, “to pray for (someone) for (something)”: li- marks the one prayed for, bi- what is asked. The two verbs chime, waddaʿahā wa-daʿā lahā. thabāt, “firmness, steadfastness”. min ʿindihā, “from her presence”. The shadda of ودّعها is printed.

sentences.t:
وَيَخْطُو لِي خَيَالُكَ فِي ضَمِيرِي * عَلَى بُعْدِ الْمَكَانِ خُطَى مَزُورِ
وَتُدْنِيكَ الْاَمَانِي مِنْ فُؤَادِي * وَاَيْنَ الْبَرْقُ مِنْ لَمْحِ الْبَصِيرِ
فَلَا تَبْعُدْ لِاَنَّكَ نُورُ عَيْنِي * اِذَا مَا غِبْتَ لَمْ تَكْمُلْ بِنُورِ
sentences.tr:
wa-yakhṭū lī khayāluka fī ḍamīrī * ʿalā buʿdi al-makāni khuṭā mazūri
wa-tudnīka al-amānī min fuʾādī * wa-ayna al-barqu min lamḥi al-baṣīri
fa-lā tabʿud li-annaka nūru ʿaynī * idhā mā ghibta lam takmul bi-nūri
sentences.l:
And-steps to-me your-phantom in my-inmost-mind, * despite (the) distance (of) the-place, (the) steps (of) one-visited.
And-bring-you-near the-hopes to my-heart; * and-where (is) the-lightning from (the) glance (of) the-seeing-one?
So-do-not be-far, because-you (are the) light (of) my-eye; * when you-are-absent, not it-is-complete with-light.
sentences.n: The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept, with hamza again as a vowel on bare alif (الْاَمَانِي, اِذَا, لِاَنَّكَ) and the ؤ of فُؤَادِي printed. Budūr speaks to the absent youth. khayāl is the phantom of the beloved that visits the lover by night; ḍamīr, “the inmost mind”. khuṭā mazūri, “the steps of one visited”: mazūr, passive participle of zāra, is the one who receives a visit, and in love poetry that is the beloved, whom the lover goes to see. Here, it seems, the one who is usually visited comes to her himself in phantom form. The reading is not certain. ayna al-barqu min …, “where is lightning beside …”: lightning is nothing to the glance of a seeing eye, so swift is the phantom’s coming. lā tabʿud, “do not be far”, is also the old wish over the dead, “may you not perish”. In the last hemistich the subject of lam takmul is ʿaynī, “my eye” (f.): when you are gone it is not filled with light. bi-nūri has the kasra without tanwīn, for the rhyme.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ مَرْزَوَانَ تَمَشَّي إِلَى بَيْتِ وَالِدَتِهِ فَنَامَ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Marzawāna tamashshā ilā bayti wālidatihi fa-nāma tilka al-laylata
sentences.l: Then indeed Marzawān walked to (the) house (of) his-mother, and-slept that the-night.
sentences.i: Then Marzawān walked to his mother’s house and slept there that night.
sentences.n: tamashshā, Form V, “to walk, make one’s way”: the print writes the final alif maqṣūra with a dotted ي, تمشي, so that it looks like the imperfect tamshī; it is kept and read as the perfect, which the sense requires. tilka al-laylata, “that night”, accusative of time.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ تَجَهَّزَ لِلسَّفَرِ فَسَافَرَ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ مُسَافِرًا مِنْ مَدِينَةٍ إِلَى مَدِينَةٍ وَمِنْ جَزِيرَةٍ إِلَى جَزِيرَةٍ مُدَّةَ شَهْرٍ كَامِلٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa tajahhaza li-al-safari fa-sāfara wa-lam yazal musāfiran min madīnatin ilā madīnatin wa-min jazīratin ilā jazīratin muddata shahrin kāmilin
sentences.l: And-when he-reached-morning, he-made-ready for-the-journey, and-travelled, and-not he-ceased travelling from a-city to a-city and-from an-island to an-island (for the) space (of) a-month complete.
sentences.i: In the morning he made ready for the road and set out, and travelled on from city to city and from island to island for a whole month.
sentences.n: tajahhaza li-, Form V, “to make ready for”: li- marks what one readies for. lam yazal, “he did not cease”, with the participle musāfiran, “travelling”: he kept on travelling. muddata, “for the space of”, accusative of time.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ مَدِينَةً يُقَالُ لَهَا الطَّيْرَبُ وَمَشَى يَسْتَنْشِقُ الْأَخْبَارَ مِنَ النَّاسِ لَعَلَّهُ يَجِدُ دَوَاءَ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala madīnatan yuqālu lahā al-Ṭayrabu wa-mashā yastanshiqu al-akhbāra mina al-nāsi laʿallahu yajidu dawāʾa al-malikati Budūra
sentences.l: Then-he-entered a-city (which) is-said to-it al-Ṭayrab, and-walked sniffing the-news from the-people; perhaps-he finds (the) remedy (of) the-queen Budūr.
sentences.i: Then he came to a city called al-Ṭayrab, and went about it sniffing out news from the people, in the hope of finding a cure for Queen Budūr.
sentences.n: yuqālu lahā, “it is said to it”, that is, which is called; li- marks what is named. The print does not point the city’s name, and the reading al-Ṭayrab is a guess. istanshaqa, Form X, “to sniff, breathe in”; istanshaqa al-akhbār, to nose out news. laʿallahu yajidu, “perhaps he finds”, with the plain imperfect this time. Budūr is malika, “queen”, here and sitt, “lady”, a few lines before; the text uses both. The ء of دواء is printed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ كُلَّمَا يَدْخُلُ مَدِينَةً أَوْ يَمُرُّ بِهَا يَسْمَعُ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَةَ بُدُورَ بِنْتَ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ قَدْ حَصَلَ لَهَا جُنُونٌ إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلَ إِلَى مَدِينَةِ الطَّيْرَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna kullamā yadkhulu madīnatan aw yamurru bihā yasmaʿu anna al-malikata Budūra binta al-maliki al-Ghayūri qad ḥaṣala lahā junūnun ilā an waṣala ilā madīnati al-Ṭayrabi
sentences.l: And-he-was, whenever he-enters a-city or passes by-it, hearing that the-queen Budūr, (the) daughter (of) the-king al-Ghayūr, had befallen to-her madness, until that he-arrived at (the) city (of) al-Ṭayrab.
sentences.i: In every city he entered or passed by, he heard that Queen Budūr, daughter of King al-Ghayūr, had gone mad, until he came to the city of al-Ṭayrab.
sentences.n: The narrator steps back to tell what Marzawān heard on the way. kullamā, “whenever”, takes the perfect in Classical Arabic; here it has the imperfect, yadkhulu, yamurru, as in the spoken language. marra bi-, “to pass by”: the verb takes its object with bi-; the shadda of يمرّ is printed. ḥaṣala li-, “to befall”: li- marks the one befallen; the verb is masculine before its subject junūn, “madness”. ilā an, “until”.

sentences.t: فَسَمِعَ خَبَرَ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ ابْنِ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ بِأَنَّهُ مَرِيضٌ وَأَنَّهُ اعْتَرَاةُ وَسْوَاسٌ وَجُنُونٌ
sentences.tr: fa-samiʿa khabara Qamari al-Zamāni ibni al-maliki Shahramāna bi-annahu marīḍun wa-annahu iʿtarāhu waswāsun wa-junūnun
sentences.l: And-he-heard (the) news (of) Qamar al-Zamān, (the) son (of) the-king Shahramān, that-he (was) sick and-that-he, came-upon-him obsession and-madness.
sentences.i: There he heard news of Qamar al-Zamān, son of King Shahramān: that he was sick, and that melancholy and madness had come upon him.
sentences.n: The two halves of the tale begin to meet. bi-annahu, “that he …”: bi- introduces what the news says, as after akhbara bi-. annahu iʿtarāhu, “that he, (it) came upon him”: the pronoun is picked up again as object; the print writes it with ة, اعتراة. waswās, “whispering”, the whisper of the devil, hence obsession, the troubled fancy of melancholy. Shahramān, a diptote, has -a for the genitive.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلَ مَرْزَوَانُ عَنِ اسْمِ مَدِينَتِهِ فَقَالُوا لَهُ إِنَّهُ فِي جَزَائِرِ خَالِدَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-saʾala Marzawānu ʿani ismi madīnatihi fa-qālū lahu innahu fī jazāʾiri Khālidāna
sentences.l: And-asked Marzawān about (the) name (of) his-city, and-they-said to-him: Indeed-he (is) in (the) Islands (of) Khālidān,
sentences.i: Marzawān asked the name of his city, and they told him, “He is in the Islands of Khālidān,
sentences.n: saʾala ʿan, “to ask about”. After qāla, inna is used, not anna: innahu, “he is”. Khālidān, the islands of King Shahramān, is a diptote, genitive in -a. The hamza of فسأل and the ئ of جزائر are printed.

sentences.t: وَهِيَ مِنْ مَدِينَتِنَا هٰذِةِ مَسِيرَةُ شَهْرٍ كَامِلٍ فِى الْبَحْرِ وَأَمَّا فِى الْبَرِّفَسِتَّةُ أَشْهُرٍ
sentences.tr: wa-hiya min madīnatinā hādhihi masīratu shahrin kāmilin fī al-baḥri wa-ammā fī al-barri fa-sittatu ashhurin
sentences.l: and-they (are) from our-city this (a) journey (of) a-month complete by the-sea; and-as-for by the-land, then-six months.
sentences.i: and they are a full month’s voyage from this city of ours by sea, and by land six months.”
sentences.n: hiya, “she”, stands for the islands, a non-human plural taking the feminine singular. masīra, “a journey of”, used of distances. fī al-baḥr, “at sea, by sea”. ammā … fa-, “as for … then”. The print runs al-barri and fa-sittatu together as one word, البرفستة; the spacing is kept. sitta, “six”, takes the plural ashhur in the genitive. hādhihi has the ة again.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَ مَرْزَوَانُ فِي مَرْكَبٍ كَانَتْ مُتَوَجِّهَةً إِلَى جَزَائِرِ خَالِدَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-nazala Marzawānu fī markabin kānat mutawajjihatan ilā jazāʾiri Khālidāna
sentences.l: So-went-down Marzawān into a-ship (that) was heading to (the) Islands (of) Khālidān,
sentences.i: So Marzawān went aboard a ship bound for the Islands of Khālidān,
sentences.n: The print has جرائر, a misprint for جزائر, “islands”, corrected here: the word is printed rightly on the lines before and after. nazala fī markabin, “to go down into a ship”, to embark. markab, “ship”, is masculine, but here takes the feminine kānat … mutawajjihatan, as ships often do in the text. tawajjaha ilā, Form V, “to head for”.

sentences.t: فَطَابَ لَهَا الرِّيحُ مُدَّةَ شَهْرٍ فَأَشْرَفُوا عَلَى جَزَائِرِ خَالِدَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭāba lahā al-rīḥu muddata shahrin fa-ashrafū ʿalā jazāʾiri Khālidāna
sentences.l: and-was-good for-her the-wind (the) space (of) a-month, and-they-looked-down on (the) Islands (of) Khālidān.
sentences.i: and the wind was fair for her for a month, and they came in sight of the Islands of Khālidān.
sentences.n: ṭāba li-, “to be good, pleasant for”: li- marks who benefits; of a wind, to be fair. rīḥ, “wind”, is usually feminine, but the verb here is masculine, as again in the next sentence. ashrafa ʿalā, Form IV, “to look down on, come in sight of”. The ئ of جزائر is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا أَشْرَفُوا عَلَيْهَا وَلَمْ يَبْقَ لَهُمْ إِلَّا الْوُصُولُ إِلَى السَّاحِلِ وَإِذَا بِرِيحٍ عَاصِفٍ خَرَجَ عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā ashrafū ʿalayhā wa-lam yabqa lahum illā al-wuṣūlu ilā al-sāḥili wa-idhā bi-rīḥin ʿāṣifin kharaja ʿalayhim
sentences.l: And-when they-looked-down on-them, and-not remained for-them except the-arriving at the-shore, and-behold, a-wind storming went-out upon-them,
sentences.i: But when they had sighted them, and nothing was left but to reach the shore, all at once a storm wind broke upon them,
sentences.n: lam yabqa, jussive of baqiya, “to remain”. wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears. The wa- before idhā, after a clause with lammā, is loose but common in the text. ʿāṣif, “violent, stormy”, an epithet that serves both genders; kharaja ʿalā, “to come out against”, is masculine with rīḥ, as before.

sentences.t: وَرَمَى الصَّوَارِيَ وَمَزَّقَ الْقُمَاشَ وَوَقَعَتِ الْقُلُوعُ فِى الْبَحْرِ وَانْقَلَبَتِ الْمَرْكَبُ بِجَمِيعِ مَا فِيهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ramā al-ṣawāriya wa-mazzaqa al-qumāsha wa-waqaʿati al-qulūʿu fī al-baḥri wa-inqalabati al-markabu bi-jamīʿi mā fīhā
sentences.l: and-threw-down the-masts and-tore the-cloth, and-fell the-sails into the-sea, and-turned-over the-ship with-all what (was) in-it.
sentences.i: brought down the masts and tore the canvas; the sails fell into the sea, and the ship turned over with everything in her.
sentences.n: ṣawārī, plural of ṣārī, “mast”. mazzaqa, Form II, “to tear to pieces”. qumāsh, “cloth”, here the canvas; qulūʿ, plural of qilʿ, “sail”. inqalaba, Form VII, “to turn over”; bi-, “with”, takes in all the ship carried. markab is feminine again. The night breaks off with the ship overturned.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
